pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.

schema.name: PowerShell
schema.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:

   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)

   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`

git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, indefinitely** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Timeout → killed. Set `persistent: true` for session-length watches (PR monitoring, log tails) — the monitor runs until you call TaskStop or the session ends. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms, max 3600000ms. Ignored when persistent is true.

persistent.description: Run for the lifetime of the session (no timeout). Use for session-length watches like PR monitoring or log tails. Stop with TaskStop.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

entries.name: SendMessage
entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will process your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

entries.name: TaskStop
entries.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID ("name@team") or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. Exception: claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) ARE fetchable via your claude.ai login — use WebFetch, not curl (curl gets the SPA shell or a Cloudflare 403).
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

entries.name: WebSearch
entries.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is September 2026 — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context7_context7__query-docs
entries.description:
Retrieves and queries up-to-date documentation and code examples from Context7 for any programming library or framework.

You must call 'Resolve Context7 Library ID' tool first to obtain the exact Context7-compatible library ID required to use this tool, UNLESS the user explicitly provides a library ID in the format '/org/project' or '/org/project/version' in their query.

Do not call this tool more than 3 times per question.

libraryId.description: Exact Context7-compatible library ID (e.g., '/mongodb/docs', '/vercel/next.js', '/supabase/supabase', '/vercel/next.js/v14.3.0-canary.87') retrieved from 'resolve-library-id' or directly from user query in the format '/org/project' or '/org/project/version'.

query.description: What to look up in the library's documentation, scoped to a single concept. Be specific and include relevant details, but keep each query to one topic — if the user's question spans multiple distinct concepts, make a separate call per concept instead of combining them, unless the question is about how the concepts interact. Good: 'How to set up authentication with JWT in Express.js' or 'React useEffect cleanup function examples'. Bad (too vague): 'auth' or 'hooks'. Bad (too broad): 'routing and auth and caching in Next.js'. The query is sent to the Context7 API for processing. Do not include any sensitive or confidential information such as API keys, passwords, credentials, personal data, or proprietary code in your query.

entries.name: mcp__plugin_context7_context7__resolve-library-id
entries.description:
Resolves a package/product name to a Context7-compatible library ID and returns matching libraries.

You MUST call this function before 'Query Documentation' tool to obtain a valid Context7-compatible library ID UNLESS the user explicitly provides a library ID in the format '/org/project' or '/org/project/version' in their query.

Each result includes:
- Library ID: Context7-compatible identifier (format: /org/project)
- Name: Library or package name
- Description: Short summary
- Code Snippets: Number of available code examples
- Source Reputation: Authority indicator (High, Medium, Low, or Unknown)
- Benchmark Score: Quality indicator (100 is the highest score)
- Versions: List of versions if available. Use one of those versions if the user provides a version in their query. The format of the version is /org/project/version.

For best results, select libraries based on name match, source reputation, snippet coverage, benchmark score, and relevance to your use case.

Selection Process:
1. Analyze the query to understand what library/package the user is looking for
2. Return the most relevant match based on:
- Name similarity to the query (exact matches prioritized)
- Description relevance to the query's intent
- Documentation coverage (prioritize libraries with higher Code Snippet counts)
- Source reputation (consider libraries with High or Medium reputation more authoritative)
- Benchmark Score: Quality indicator (100 is the highest score)

Response Format:
- Return the selected library ID in a clearly marked section
- Provide a brief explanation for why this library was chosen
- If multiple good matches exist, acknowledge this but proceed with the most relevant one
- If no good matches exist, clearly state this and suggest query refinements

For ambiguous queries, request clarification before proceeding with a best-guess match.

IMPORTANT: Do not call this tool more than 3 times per question. If you cannot find what you need after 3 calls, use the best result you have.

query.description: What to look up in the library's documentation. This is used to rank library results by relevance to what the user is trying to accomplish. The query is sent to the Context7 API for processing. Do not include any sensitive or confidential information such as API keys, passwords, credentials, personal data, or proprietary code in your query.

libraryName.description: Library name to search for and retrieve a Context7-compatible library ID. Use the official library name with proper punctuation — e.g., 'Next.js' instead of 'nextjs', 'Customer.io' instead of 'customerio', 'Three.js' instead of 'threejs'.

entries.name: mcp__workos__list_operations
entries.description: Discover the WorkOS operations available through the query and mutate tools. Without arguments, returns the full index of operation names — call it once and reuse the result. Pass filter to narrow the index by keyword (operation name or description). Pass operation for that operation’s parameters and input types, or type to fully expand a specific input/enum type by name. Call whoami to see available environments and their IDs.

operation.description: An operation name from the index to get its parameters and input types.

type.description: An input or enum type name (e.g. one named in an operation’s parameters) to fully expand — use this to resolve deeply nested input shapes without triggering an error.

filter.description: Case-insensitive keyword to narrow the index by operation name or description, e.g. "branding", "sso", "organization".

entries.name: mcp__workos__mutate
entries.description: Run a mutation against your WorkOS account by name. Mutations change real data in the targeted environment. Call list_operations first to discover available operations and their parameters. ### Task 13: Icons, docs, packaging, Marketplace

**Files:**

- Create: `streamdeck/com.scrthq.runlog.sdPlugin/imgs/**` (plugin, category, five action icons at 20/40 and 72/144 — SVG source in `streamdeck/design/`, exported PNG)
- Create: `apps/web/src/guide/pages/stream-deck.mdx`; modify `apps/web/src/guide/pages.ts` and `streaming.mdx`'s "Where to go next"
- Modify: `docs/stream-api.md` (the deck section from Plan A gains "or use the plugin")
- Modify: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (`streamdeck pack` on tags, artifact upload)
- Create: `streamdeck/README.md` (the Marketplace listing text)

**Interfaces:**

- Produces: a `.streamDeckPlugin` from CI on every release tag, and a submission on the Elgato Maker portal.

- [ ] **Step 1: Icons**

Draw the seven icons in the app's palette (celadon `#4d8a6f` on the dark ground, kiln for Undo) as SVG in `streamdeck/design/`, export PNG at both sizes with `npx @resvg/resvg-cli` (a dev dependency at the root, not in the plugin). Category and plugin icons are the Runlog mark.

- [ ] **Step 2: The guide page**

`stream-deck.mdx`, in the voice of `dock.mdx`: install from the Marketplace, sign in from any key's settings, what the Run key does, which keys exist, that a run must be synced and open in a browser, and that pressing is part of Plus. No paragraph about why a deck is good.

- [ ] **Step 3: Pack in CI**

Add to the `deck` job on `v*` tags: `npx streamdeck pack streamdeck/com.scrthq.runlog.sdPlugin -o dist/` and upload `dist/*.streamDeckPlugin` as a workflow artifact and a release asset.

- [ ] **Step 4: Submit**

On the Elgato Maker portal: upload the packed plugin, the listing text from `streamdeck/README.md`, screenshots of the profile on a MK.2 and a +. Record the submission id and status in the `plan-artifacts` memory under this plan's entry.

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
npm run typecheck && npm run lint:docs && npx vitest run streamdeck apps/web/src/guide
git add streamdeck apps/web/src/guide docs/stream-api.md .github/workflows/ci.yml
git commit -m "feat(deck): icons, the guide page, and the packed plugin"
```

---

## Self-review

**Spec coverage.** Sign-in via device flow on a client of its own (3, 8) · `packages/session/` extraction (4) · the workspace, Node 24 / SD 7.1, pinned SDK (5) · five actions (10, 11, 12) · faces as base64 SVG, no rasterizer (7) · the runs list pushed and the three attach states (6, 9) · pinning beats following, ended pinned run says so (6, 11) · `switchToProfile` on attach, `showOk`, the page's toast is Plan A Task 10 (11) · socket life follows configuration (10) · *Not synced* (1, 6) · the Plus refusal drawn from `drove` with no client-side gate (6, 9) · Encoder and Neo (12) · Marketplace (13). **Gap found and closed here:** the spec never said how the deck *reads* the numbers; Task 2 adds a member `GET` on the snapshot and Task 9 fetches it on the doorbell — the deck watches its attached run on the same socket, and `writes()` from Plan A already excludes a deck from counting as a writer.

**Placeholder scan.** Task 5's manifest is marked as subject to `streamdeck validate`; Task 12's custom layout is conditional on `$B1` being too plain, with the fallback stated. No TBDs.

**Type consistency.** `DeckState`/`DeckEvent`/`Face` (6) are consumed unchanged by 7, 9, 10, 11, 12. `Wire.press` returns the `ref` (9) that `RunlogAction.send` (10) matches against `flash.ref`. `HeldRun` (6) matches the `runs` message shape from Plan A Task 3 plus `any` from Task 1 here. `PressTarget` and `MetricField` (6) are the settings types in 10 and 12.

---

      - run: npm run build

  # The Stream Deck plugin: its own workspace, built and validated on its
  # own, since neither the build nor the manifest shape has anything to do
  # with the app's suite above. Nothing is packed or published here; that
  # is Task 13's job.
  Deck:
    name: Stream Deck plugin
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    if: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' || github.event_name == 'merge_group' || github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Setup Node and run npm ci
        uses: ./.github/actions/npm-ci
        with:
          node-version: ${{ env.NODE_VERSION }}

      - run: npm run build -w streamdeck
      - run: npx --workspace streamdeck streamdeck validate com.scrthq.runlog.sdPlugin

  InfraTest:
    name: Test the hosting
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    if: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' || github.event_name == 'merge_group' || github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' }}
    strategy:
      matrix:
        aws-environment: [dev, prd]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Setup Node and run npm ci
        uses: ./.github/actions/npm-ci
        with:
          node-version: ${{ env.NODE_VERSION }}

      # No credentials, and no real account: the stacks are asserted against
      # a synthesized template, so the tests need an account id to render
      # into ARNs and nothing more. A stand-in does that on a fork's pull
      # request as well as here, and keeps the real ids out of the picture.
---
            style
            test
            build
            ci
            chore
            revert
          scopes: |
            run
            designer

            profile

# A dock for the controls

OBS can keep a signed-in web page docked beside the preview: **View** → **Docks** → **Custom Browser Docks**. Give it a name ("Runlog") and, from the run's Stream panel, **Copy dock address**: it is the run's remote alone on a page (the next move, the last result, undo). **Apply**, and sign in inside the dock, once; OBS keeps that sign-in between sessions, and the address survives the trip through the sign-in service and back.

## A second device at your table

The dock is a second device, so the run must be on it: on the machine you play on it already is, and on another it arrives through sync once you are signed in there. A move you make in the dock is on your other screens in a moment.

The dock announces nothing of its own to the stream (no dice and no ticker lines); the page it stands beside does that, so the two do not say the same thing twice.

## The whole app in a dock

# place in the queue (GitHub keeps one pending run per lane, the newest),
  # so approving the newest releases everything merged so far, once. What
  # a superseded run would have tagged, the newer one tags; a number already
  # taken is refused rather than reused.
  Release:
    name: Tag and publish
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    needs: DevDeploy
    environment: release
    permissions:
      contents: read
    concurrency:
      group: release
      cancel-in-progress: true
    steps:
          OUTPUT: RELEASE_NOTES.md
      - name: Write the whole changelog
        uses: orhun/git-cliff-action@v4
        with:
          config: cliff.toml
          args: --tag ${{ steps.release.outputs.next }}
        env:
          OUTPUT: CHANGELOG.md

      - name: Tag and publish
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          gh release create "${{ steps.release.outputs.next }}" \
            --target "${{ github.sha }}" \
            --title "${{ steps.release.outputs.next }}" \
            --notes-file RELEASE_NOTES.md \
            --latest \
            CHANGELOG.md

          {
            echo "### Released ${{ steps.release.outputs.next }}"
            echo ""
            if [ -n "${{ steps.release.outputs.moved }}" ]; then echo "The number moved on the way: ${{ steps.release.outputs.moved }}, because a release approved in between took the one dev was built with."; echo ""; fi
            echo "Production deploys from the release event."
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

content.text:
That loop is the pack, not the plugin. I pulled the run's snapshot to check: the step is `Play` (a `manual` step with a checklist), and the offer the page is publishing is exactly what your two keys are pressing:

- **"I settled it"** (your Press key) is an `anytime` move in `elden-ring-tarnishedtool.yaml:1732` whose only effect is `rollOn: blessing`. It doesn't advance anything — every press draws another blessing, which is the seven Blessing entries in your log (Hurried, Second wind, Held, …).
- **"Press to Roll"** (the follow key) then correctly offers that pending Blessing roll and rolls it — that's the #292 fix working live (`offer.primary = { id: "roll", label: "Blessing" }` in the snapshot).

Neither key ends the Play step, because the step is a checklist: "The curse is in force / The objective was named… / If you settled it… / You were moved…". By the hands-free rule, the follow key never ticks a list on its own — after the roll it goes back to saying the step is on the page. Two ways past it from the deck:

1. Set a Press key to **"Tick everything and Next"** — it appears in the Press key's settings list while the run is on a checklist step (the widget you asked for). One press ticks the four boxes and moves to End the scene.
2. Tick on the page as usual.

Two things I'd change, your call:

- In the pack, `settled` probably wants to be once per scene (`available` already has `unitIndex gte 1`; adding a once-per-unit guard stops a second blessing draw). That's your sketch pack, so I'll leave it unless you say so.
- The follow key could carry an opt-in on its own settings — "on a checklist step, tick everything" — so one key runs a whole scene. It would be the streamer choosing to skip the reading, which the rule allows. Say the word and I'll add it as a task.

Meanwhile Task 13 passed review (one wording fix from me, `09e769d`): icons, the guide page, the packed plugin on every release, and the `deck` PR scope are all on the branch. Left before the plugin PR: your exported Runlog profile (for the `Profiles` manifest entry), the whole-branch review, and your answers on the Metric face and the run-picker/openUrl question.

Yes — Next is the "do the next thing" key: it presses whatever the run is waiting on right now. Reading the run's published offer this minute: a **Blessing** roll is still pending (from the last "I settled it"), so Next should show **Blessing** and a press should roll it, the same as the page's "Roll for me". The offer hasn't changed since 23:34 (`seq` 53), so no press has landed on the page in half an hour.

Two cases, depending on what the key says:

- **It shows "Blessing" and pressing does nothing** — the page isn't taking the press. The deck goes through the browser tab holding the run, and Chrome puts a background tab to sleep; click into the run's tab (the pending Blessing panel with "Roll for me" should be visible) and press Next again. That's the tab-discard problem from earlier, and it's why I want the guide to say keep the run in an OBS dock or exempt the site from Memory Saver.
- **It shows "Play the scene… on the page"** — that's by design at a checklist step: Next won't tick a list for you, so it refuses and says where the step is. A Press key set to "Tick everything and Next" is the one that finishes the scene from the deck (I'll add a Next-key opt-in for that if you want it).

What does the Next key's face say, and what does it flash when you press it (the flash is the verdict — "That moved on.", "The run is not asking for that.", etc.)?

content.text:
That's a cleaner rule for the key: **Next does the next logical thing, decisions included, unless you tell it to stop at them.** Here's what I'd build — say yes and I'll dispatch it as the next plugin task.

**What Next presses, in order**

1. What it does today: a pending roll, the step's roll, carry on, close the unit, enter the next one.
2. **A checklist step** → "Tick everything and Next" (the preset that's already on offer; the page ticks the list and presses the step's own button).
3. **A declaration step** (name a subject, etc.) → the first suggestion the run makes — the words the dice used, or the step's own table — sent as the answer. With no suggestion on offer, it still says "on the page", since there's nothing to take.
4. Something owed, an ended run, a question the pack asks the player (`ask`/`prompt`/`chooseTarget`) → still "on the page". Those need words or a judgement the run can't supply.

**The opt-out**: one checkbox in the Next key's settings, *Stop at decisions* (off by default), which puts 2 and 3 back to "on the page". Placing the key and leaving it unchecked is the streamer's choice to skip the reading, which keeps the hands-free rule intact.

**The face** shows what it'll do: "Blessing", "Carry on", "Tick everything and Next", or "Name it · Exalted Flesh" (wrapped), so you can see the decision before you press it.

**Where it lives**: plugin only (`next.ts`, `state.ts`, `ui/next.html`) — the page already offers both presets and `takePress` already takes them, so nothing new ships to the app or the server, and it goes in the plugin PR.

The one thing I'd hold back: the pack's "I settled it" is `anytime`, so Next won't press it (a move is a claim about what happened at the table, not ceremony); you'd still press Settled once, and Next takes it from there — Blessing roll, tick the list, End the scene, next scene, Curse roll…

Good to go?

content.text:
Three things, in order of what I need from you.

**Metric key — instrumented, need one press.** The `streamdeck restart` command was being acknowledged but not honored (the plugin process was still the 23:25 one), so I killed it and the app relaunched it on the current build, which now logs what every key says whenever it changes. The Metric key came up with its setting intact — `{"field":{"resource":"warpEvery"}}`, "Scenes before a warp" — and I've simulated its face with the live run's numbers: it should draw **4/10** with the label beneath. Press **Connect** once and I'll read the log; if the face still doesn't show, the log now says exactly what the key was told to draw.

**Setup on press — yes, and here's the shape.** The page already has both halves in Settings: choose a setup (`run.setSetup`) and *Hand out* (the `setup` gesture the tool acts on). So:

- The offer gains `setups: [{ id, title }]` — the setups in your library for the pack's tool (Brute, Cleric, Give runes…).
- The Press key gets a fourth target, **Apply a setup**, listing them by title in its settings; the face shows the title.
- A press sends `{ press: "setup", id }`; the page sets the run's setup to that one and hands it out in the same act, so one press changes the loadout in the game. Refused with "That setup is not here" if the library no longer has it.
- Not on Next: switching a loadout is a decision, not ceremony.

**Next as the one button** — still waiting on your yes to the design above (decisions included by default, *Stop at decisions* checkbox to opt out). If both are a go, they're the next two plugin tasks, in that order.

### Task 14: The page keeps its doorbell while its tab is hidden

Found live 2026-09-15 00:24: switching the browser tab away from the run made the deck lose it. Cause: `apps/web/src/sync/SyncProvider.tsx` `onVisibleSocket` closes the live socket the moment the document is hidden (`else closeSocket()`), and `openSocket` refuses to open unless visible. The socket is what holds the run for a deck (`writes()` on the server counts a page's watching connection), so a hidden tab drops the hold. Streamers keep the run's tab behind OBS, behind the game, or on another monitor; hidden is the normal state, not the exception.

**Files:**
- Modify: `apps/web/src/sync/SyncProvider.tsx`
- Test: `apps/web/src/sync/sync.test.ts` if it renders the provider with a fake socket; otherwise the nearest test that exercises `openLive`/visibility, or a new `SyncProvider.visibility.test.tsx` beside it using the same fakes the existing tests use (`socket.test.ts` shows the `openLive` fake shape).
- Modify: `docs/stream-api.md` only if it states that a page's hold ends when its tab is hidden (grep "visible"/"hidden"); otherwise no doc change.

**Rule:** the doorbell socket stays open for as long as a run is open, hidden or not. Visibility still gates the *poll* (a hidden tab does not fetch on a timer) and the `focus`/`visible` wake still syncs at once. Concretely:
- `openSocket()`: drop the `document.visibilityState !== "visible"` condition; keep `if (socket || !lastActive()) return;`.
- `onVisibleSocket`: on visible → `openSocket()`; on hidden → nothing. (Do not delete the listener; a tab that was hidden at mount with a run arriving later still needs the open on visible, and the poll's `openSocket()` call stays as the backstop.)
- The comment above the socket block says "one socket while the page is visible and a run is open" — rewrite it to say the socket stays up while a run is open, hidden or not, and why (a deck presses through this page; a hidden tab is where a streamer keeps it).
- Nothing else changes: `closeSocket()` on unmount and when the run closes (the poll/`watchCurrent` path) as today.

**Tests (write first, see them fail):**
1. Mount with an active run, socket opened (fake `openLive` records calls). Dispatch `visibilitychange` with `document.visibilityState` stubbed to `"hidden"` → the fake socket's `close` was NOT called.
2. Mount while `"hidden"` with an active run → the socket is opened anyway (`openLive` called once).
3. Unmount → `close` called (unchanged behavior, keeps the regression net).

**Checks:** `npx vitest run apps/web/src/sync`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run format:check`.

**Commit:** `fix(live): the page keeps its doorbell while its tab is hidden`. No trailers, no footer.

Branch: `the-page-stays-held`, off `origin/main`, as its own PR with auto-merge (`live` is an allowed scope).
EOF
cat > $W/task-15-brief.md <<'EOF'
### Task 15: Next takes the decisions too, and the faces get bigger

The user's rule for the follow key (2026-09-15 00:09): "one button that can keep you moving through a simple run" — roll, carry on, close, enter, and at a checklist or a declaration, take the preset the page already offers. Placing the key and leaving *Stop at decisions* unchecked is the streamer choosing to skip the reading, which is what `handsFree.ts`'s rule asks for. Plugin only: the page already publishes both presets in `offer.presets` and `takePress` already takes them.

**Files:**
- Modify: `streamdeck/src/state.ts` (`nextFace`, a new pure `nextPress`), `streamdeck/src/state.test.ts`
- Modify: `streamdeck/src/actions/next.ts` (settings type, `onKeyDown`/`onDialDown` use `nextPress`), `streamdeck/src/actions/next.test.ts` (create if absent; mock `../plugin.ts` the way `metric.test.ts` does)
- Modify: `streamdeck/com.scrthq.runlog.sdPlugin/ui/next.html` (one checkbox, saved as `{ stop: true }` via `streamDeckClient.setSettings`; read back with `getSettings` — see `ui/metric.html` for the v4 client shape; no `streamDeckClient.on`, it does not exist)
- Modify: `streamdeck/src/face.ts`, `streamdeck/src/face.test.ts` (bigger type)
- Modify: `streamdeck/com.scrthq.runlog.sdPlugin/manifest.json` — the Next action's `Tooltip` gains "and takes the decisions unless told to stop"; nothing else.
- Docs: `apps/web/src/guide/pages/stream-deck.mdx` — the Next key's paragraph says it takes a checklist and a declaration's first suggestion, and names the *Stop at decisions* setting. One home per fact; nothing elsewhere.

**Interfaces:**
- `export type NextSettings = { stop?: boolean }` in `next.ts`.
- `export function nextPress(state: DeckState, settings: NextSettings): { press: "primary" } | { press: "answer"; answer: Record<string, string> } | null` in `state.ts`. Order:
  1. `offer.primary` → `{ press: "primary" }`.
  2. Unless `settings.stop`: a preset with `kind === "checklist"` → `{ press: "answer", answer: { checklist: "" } }` (what `press.ts` sends for that preset today — read `press.ts:27` and match the key it uses exactly); a preset with `kind === "declareSubject"` whose `suggestions[0]` exists → `{ press: "answer", answer: { subject: suggestions[0] } }`.
  3. Otherwise `null`.
- `nextFace(state, settings)` shows what `nextPress` would do: the primary's label; the checklist preset's label ("Tick everything and Next" — the page's words, use `preset.label`); for a declaration `{ title: suggestions[0], when: preset.label }` (the `when` line carries "Name what you are going for" trimmed as `face.ts` already trims); with `stop` or nothing to take, the existing `needsPage` face. `nextFace`'s existing signature gains the settings parameter; update its callers and tests.
- `next.ts` `onKeyDown`/`onDialDown`: `const p = nextPress(store.state, ev.payload.settings); if (!p) return this.flashRefused(...)` — look at how a refused press is shown today (`RunlogAction.send` and `flash`); if there is no local-refusal path, send `{ press: "primary" }` as today and let the page refuse with its `needsPage`, which the face already shows. Prefer the local path only if it is one or two lines.
- Faces (`face.ts`): the title's type scale goes up one step across the board — currently a size chosen from line count (34 for one short line, 20 for wrapped); make it 40 / 30 / 22 for one / two / three lines with `wrap(text, width, 3)` choosing width by size (roughly 7 / 9 / 12 characters per line at those sizes in a 144px face with 12px side padding). Long phrases wrap to up to three lines; a phrase longer than three lines is ellipsized on the last line, never clipped by the frame. The `when` line stays 12px. Keep the `<title>` with the full text. Update `face.test.ts` expectations and add: a 30-character phrase yields three lines and no line wider than its width; a one-word title is size 40.

**Tests first**, then implement, then `npx vitest run streamdeck`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint:docs`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run build -w streamdeck`, `npx --workspace streamdeck streamdeck validate com.scrthq.runlog.sdPlugin`. Do NOT restart the plugin or the Stream Deck app; the controller does that.

**Commit:** `feat(deck): the next key takes the decisions too`. No trailers, no footer.
EOF

### Task 17: Undo says Undo, and the built-in faces get as big as the frame allows

Asked 2026-09-15 00:59: "make the Undo button just say Undo" and "font size needs to be increased on all the built-in button text still". The scale from Task 15 counts characters (5/7/10 per line at 40/30/22), which is honest for the widest words and pessimistic for most: "connected" is nine narrow letters and would fit at 26px, but the count sends it to 22. Measure instead of count.

**Files:**
- Modify: `streamdeck/src/face.ts`, `streamdeck/src/face.test.ts`
- Modify: `streamdeck/src/state.ts` (`undoFace`), `streamdeck/src/state.test.ts`
- Docs: none (the guide does not describe type sizes; the Undo key's paragraph in `apps/web/src/guide/pages/stream-deck.mdx` must not claim the key shows what it would take back — read it and trim if it does).

**Undo:** `undoFace` returns `{ title: "Undo", tone: "live" }` when `offer.undo` exists and `{ title: "Undo", tone: "dim" }` otherwise. No `when`. The `common()`/`flashed()` gating stays as it is.

**Measuring:** add to `face.ts` a `measure(text: string, size: number): number` — the width in px of a line at that size, from a glyph table for the face's system sans at weight 600 in em units: narrow `i j l ' . , : ; ! | ` = 0.28; `f t r I` = 0.36; `space` = 0.28; digits and most lowercase = 0.55; `m w` = 0.85; capitals other than `I` = 0.68; `M W` = 0.92; `…` = 0.9; anything else 0.6. message.content: what does pressing Settled do from the Stream Deck?

content.text:
Exactly what pressing **I settled it** on the page does — the key is set to that move (`target: { kind: "move", id: "settled" }`), so a press sends `{ press: "move", move: "settled" }` and the page takes the move as if you'd clicked it: the pack's `settled` move (`elden-ring-tarnishedtool.yaml:1732`) runs its one effect, `rollOn: blessing`, which starts a Blessing roll. In a hands-free unit that roll waits for dice, so the run's offer becomes "roll Blessing" and the Next key reads **Blessing**; press Next and it rolls the page's own machine dice, logged as machine-rolled, and the blessing lands in the log (that's the "Whetted / Mending" chips you saw).

It does not advance the step, tick the checklist, or award anything by itself — by the pack's rules the move is `anytime` and repeatable, so every press draws another blessing. That's why the earlier loop looked endless: Settled → Blessing → Settled → Blessing. The scene ends from the Play step's checklist, which Next now takes ("Tick everything and Next") since Task 15.

If you want Settled to be a once-per-scene thing, that's a pack change (a guard on the move), not a deck change — say so and I'll add it.

content.content:
import type { Face, Tone } from "./state";

/**
 * A key face as SVG.
 *
 * SVG, because it needs no rasterizer and no native module in a package
 * the Marketplace installs; base64, because Stream Deck 7.5 on Windows
 * rejects a raw SVG string despite the documentation. 144 square is the
 * @2x size; the software scales it to any key.
 *
 * The palette is the app's own: celadon for a live key, kiln for a
 * refusal, the muted ink for a key with nothing to do. System sans, since

content.text:
That was the Metric bug, and it was every key's bug: the number/title lines were `<tspan>`s positioned inside one `<text>` with `dominant-baseline`, which the Stream Deck's SVG renderer (a Qt subset) silently drops — only the small plain-positioned label beneath ever drew. That's why you saw "Deaths" tiny and no `0`, and why the built-in text looked "super small": you were only ever seeing the 12px caption. Fixed in `f2b9ee8` — each line is now its own positioned `<text>` with an explicit baseline and a plain font stack — and the deck is restarted on it. Press **Connect**: the Metric keys should show `1 scenes` / `2` / `0` at 40px, and every other key its actual text at 26–40px.

Also landed while that was going: Task 19a (deck rolls animate on the page, verdict waits for the dice — `b585ce3`, under review), Task 20 (Next = Carry on at the receipts) now implementing on top of it, and Task 18 (Apply setup key) still implementing.

---

## Summary

`the-deck-arrives` adds a well-built Stream Deck plugin: 29 commits, ~5,300 added lines, eight actions, and a clean separation between a pure reducer (`state.ts`) and a thin SDK shell. All six verification commands pass — 105 tests across 12 files, typecheck, `lint:docs` (0 issues/93 files), `format:check`, `npm run build -w streamdeck`, and `streamdeck validate` reports **Validation successful**. The architecture is the best part of this branch: every key face is a pure function of one state object, and `state.test.ts` has a case per face. The socket's generation counter, with tests for a superseded dial, a retired close, and a late snapshot, catches a class of reconnect bug that normally ships.

Two things stop it. First, `bearer()` has no single-flight guard around a **rotating** refresh token, so two overlapping calls — routine during play — produce a spurious "Sign in again" mid-run. Second, **the branch is four commits behind `origin/main`, and those four commits (#291–#294) are the page half this plugin presses against**: `offer.setups` and `takePress`'s `setup` branch exist only on main. The merge is clean (`git merge-tree` produces a tree with no conflicts), but nothing here has been built or tested against what will actually ship. Note also that the review diff `e4c50ac..b6e8b06` is misleading — `e4c50ac` is not an ancestor of HEAD (merge-base is `ecb2fc2`), so the ~718 deletions it shows in `apps/web/src/run/` are main's work, not reverts on this branch. I reviewed against `ecb2fc2..b6e8b06`.

## Findings

### Critical

**1. Concurrent renewal burns the rotating refresh token — `streamdeck/src/session.ts:70-84`**

`bearer()` reads the session off disk, and if `needsRenewal` is true calls `renew()` with no guard. Two callers can be in flight at once: `openWire.open()` (`socket.ts:86`) and `fetchSnapshot()` (`socket.ts:59`), and `fetchSnapshot` fires on every `changed` ring. Two rings in the same turn — a roll that publishes twice — both read the same `refreshToken` and both POST it. WorkOS rotates on every renewal, so the second is refused. In `fetchSnapshot` that silently drops a snapshot (recoverable). In `open()` the refusal returns `null`, which dispatches `{ t: "session", state: "expired" }` (`socket.ts:93`) and `reduce` resets to `initial()` — the whole deck goes to **Sign in again** while the session is in fact fine. Where the issuer treats refresh-token reuse as a compromise signal, it becomes a real sign-out mid-stream.

The 60-second `RENEW_MARGIN_MS` against a 1-hour token means this window opens once an hour of active play. Smallest fix — share the in-flight promise:

```ts
let renewing: Promise<string | null> | null = null;
export async function bearer(_account: Account): Promise<string | null> {
  const session = loadSession();
  if (!session) return null;
  if (!needsRenewal(session, Date.now())) return session.accessToken;
  renewing ??= renew(session)
    .then((r) => (writeSession(dir(), r), r.accessToken))
    .catch(() => null)
    .finally(() => { renewing = null; });
  return renewing;
}
```

`session.test.ts:49` already proves rotation is written back; add a case that fires two `bearer()` calls and asserts `fetch` was called once.

**2. The branch does not carry the page half it presses — needs `origin/main` merged in**

`streamdeck/src/actions/setup.ts:22` sends `{ press: "answer", answer: { setup: id } }`, and `state.ts:26` declares `setups` on the mirrored `Offer`. On this branch, `apps/web/src/run/offer.ts` has no `setups` field and `takePress.ts` has no `setup` branch — an Apply setup press would fall through to the `declareSubject` check and come back *"The run is not asking for that."* On `e4c50ac` both exist (`offer.ts:26`, `takePress.ts:89-94`). Merge `origin/main` before opening so CI runs against the real pair. The merge itself is clean.

### Important

**3. `redrawAll` swallows nothing and catches nothing — `streamdeck/src/actions/base.ts:100-102`**

```ts
for (const a of this.actions) void a.getSettings<S>().then((s) => this.draw(a, s));
```

No `.catch`. `draw()` guards only the key branch (`base.ts:81-88`); `this.face(...)` at line 73 and `await action.setFeedback(feedback)` at line 96 are both unguarded, and `face()` reads a snapshot cast `as never` straight off the wire (`socket.ts:65`) with no validation. The SDK installs `process.once("uncaughtException")` (`dist/plugin/logging/index.js:27`) — `once`, so the first rejection is logged and the second takes the plugin down. Add `.catch((e) => streamDeck.logger.error(...))` on line 101 and move the dial branch inside the existing try.

**4. Every inspector depends on a third-party CDN at load — all eight `ui/*.html`, e.g. `press.html:6`**

`<script src="https://sdpi-components.dev/releases/v4/sdpi-components.js">`, with no `integrity` and no version beyond `v4`. Offline, or if that host is down, `const { streamDeckClient } = SDPIComponents;` throws before anything renders — the account block, the run picker, the field picker and the setup picker are all dead, so the streamer cannot even sign in. For a Marketplace plugin, vendor the file into `ui/` (it is one JS file, no build) or at minimum pin an exact release with `integrity` + `crossorigin`.

**5. `base.ts` and `plugin.ts` have no tests, and both hold logic that fails silently**

- `send()` (`base.ts:113-141`) is the only thing between a press and the streamer knowing what happened: `showOk` on a verdict, `showAlert` on a refusal, the `VERDICT_MS` fallback alert, and the cancel-on-deck-off. None of it is exercised — the action tests mock `../plugin.ts` so the subscription never receives a flash.
- `codeFromLines()` (`plugin.ts:132-140`) parses `packages/session/src/flow.ts:104-105`'s exact output with `/^ {2}Open {2}(\S+)$/` and `/^ {2}Code {2}(\S.*)$/`. It matches today, but `flow.ts` is shared with the CLI; reword either line and the sign-in code never reaches the inspector, with nothing to catch it. Export it and assert it against real `deviceFlow` `say` output.
- `connect.ts` and `undo.ts` have no press test, unlike the other six actions.

### Minor

6. `streamdeck/package.json:1` has no `"name"` and no `"private": true`, unlike every other workspace.
7. Every build prints `TS5096: allowImportingTsExtensions can only be used when noEmit or emitDeclarationOnly is set`. Noise that trains people to ignore the build's warnings.
8. `streamdeck/src/face.ts:1` imports `from "./state"` with no `.ts`; the other eleven modules all use `./state.ts`.
9. `rollup.config.mjs:38` — `include: ["src/**/*.ts", "../packages/**/src/**/*.ts"]` type-checks every package in the repo during the deck build. Only `packages/session` is imported; narrow it.
10. `CI-CD.yml:509` hard-codes `streamdeck/dist/com.scrthq.runlog.streamDeckPlugin`. I traced `@elgato/cli` 1.9.0 (`bin/streamdeck.mjs`, `cd()` strips `.sdPlugin`) and the name is right — but the Deck job never packs, so the first proof is a release that either works or fails at `gh release create`. Use `streamdeck/dist/*.streamDeckPlugin`, or add a pack step to the Deck job.
11. `base.ts:52` and `:76-78` log the face title and `JSON.stringify(settings)` at `info` — the pack's own words (move labels, run names, pack titles, a declared subject) go into the plugin log. No token is logged, which is the part that matters, but worth knowing before sending logs to Elgato support.
12. `base.ts:57` unsubscribes on `this.actions.length === 0`. `actions` is the *visible* set; if the disappearing action is still counted there, the subscription is never released. Harmless, but the intent deserves an assertion.
13. `press.html:62` saves the typed answer on `change`, so a value typed and left without blurring is lost.
14. `packages/session/src/store.ts:12` drops the `darwin` branch the plan specified (`~/Library/Application Support`). I checked `e4c50ac:packages/cli/src/account.ts:58` — the CLI had no darwin branch either, so this is a faithful move and no macOS session is stranded. Flagging only because it departs from the written plan.
15. `writeSession` (`store.ts:39-48`) is a non-atomic `writeFileSync`; a crash mid-write leaves an unreadable session and a forced re-sign-in. Temp-then-rename removes it.
16. `pin()` (`run.ts:47`) read-modify-writes global settings, which can clobber an `apiBase` the inspector is writing at the same moment.

## What is good

- **`state.ts`.** Every face is a pure function of one reducer's state, with a test per case. This is what makes the whole branch reviewable, and the `?? []` guard in `setupFace` for an older page's offer is exactly the right instinct.
- **The generation counter in `socket.ts`**, with tests named for a superseded dial's refusal, a retired socket's close, and a snapshot that arrives after its connection is gone.

Plus three worth doing in the same pass: catch errors in the redraw loop, vendor the `sdpi-components` script instead of loading it from a CDN (offline = no inspector, no sign-in), and tests for the press-verdict path and the sign-in code parser. message.content: what about the issue with the Deck connection dying when the active browser tab is changed away from the run?

content.text:
That one shipped earlier as #293 (merged and on dev at 00:55): the page used to close its live socket the moment its tab was hidden, and that socket is what holds the run for the deck. Now it stays open while a run is open, hidden or not; only the timed poll waits for a visible tab. If you were still seeing the drop after that, it's most likely the same stale-tab reason — the open tab was still running the pre-#293 bundle. The reload you're about to do for #295 picks both up.

Two things can still take the deck off the run after that, and neither is the tab switch itself:

- **Chrome discarding the tab** (Memory Saver) — the page is gone, not hidden, so nothing holds the run. Keep the run in an OBS dock or browser source, or exempt `runlog.dev.scrthq.com` / `runlog.scrthq.com` from Memory Saver; the guide says so.
- **The socket's own 2-hour limit** on API Gateway — the page reconnects with backoff, so the deck sees a few seconds of "No run open" and comes back.

If it still dies on a plain tab switch after the reload, tell me and I'll pull the deck's log and the page's console — that would be a different cause.

content.text:
Good — that confirms it was the stale bundle. On lifetimes, there are three clocks, and only one is activity-based:

- **The deck's own idle-off (activity-based, 30 minutes):** the plugin closes its socket after thirty minutes of holding *no run* — signed in, connected, but nothing open on a page. While it's following a run, that clock is off: it stays up for the whole stream. Connect then reads *went idle* beneath it, and one press reopens.
- **The page's socket (no timeout of its own now):** since #293 it stays open while a run is open, hidden or not — no activity timer. The only things that end it are closing the tab, Chrome discarding the tab, or the run being closed.
- **API Gateway's hard cap (2 hours, and 10 minutes idle at the transport layer):** every WebSocket connection is cut at two hours regardless, and one with no frames in either direction for ten minutes is dropped. Both the page and the deck reconnect on their own with backoff (1 s → 30 s); the deck sees a brief "No run open" / "Offline" while that happens. A busy run sends frames constantly; a quiet one — a Play step with nobody pressing anything for ten minutes — may hit the idle cut. The server-side rows have a two-hour TTL to match the cap.

The ten-minute transport idle is the one worth a keepalive: a tiny ping every few minutes from the page and the deck would keep a quiet Play step from reconnecting mid-scene. Not on the list yet; say the word and I'll add it to the fix round or as a follow-up.

The final fix round is running now on the plugin branch (renewal single-flight, main merged in, redraw guard, vendored inspector script, the missing tests, the small line at 16px). The deck is restarted on Task 21 meanwhile — Connect/Disconnect wording and the bigger caption are live if you reconnect once more.
